extracted.intended_audience: general_readers interested in international affairs / United Nations reporting
extracted.subtask_description: A historical Associated Press news article reporting on multiple international-diplomatic issues (United Nations debates, Balkan border commission, freedom of information, aerial inspection proposals, Indonesian–Dutch fighting). Intended to inform general readers about diplomatic disputes and UN procedural controversies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of information and press as essential to international peace
rubrics_metrics.description: The principles of freedom of information and of the press are essential to the maintenance of international peace and other objectives of the United Nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A world conference on freedom of information was recommended; governments and delegates urged removal of existing barriers to information as vital to preserving democracy and peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barriers to freedom of information (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Censorship of outgoing news, internal censorship, prohibition of imported books and periodicals, and denial of visas for foreign correspondents are barriers to freedom of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These practices were described as dangerous and as undermining the maintenance of international peace; delegates stressed such barriers should be removed and considered in membership/moral assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aerial survey procedural safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Before an aerial survey is conducted the nation concerned 'shall have notice of each aerial survey, with an opportunity to present objections or suggest modifications' and it shall have 'the right to examine the plane used and to send at least one observer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed as part of inspection arrangements (e.g., for atomic-energy controls); intended to protect sovereignty and provide transparency when international agencies conduct aerial inspections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aerial survey scope limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Aerial surveys by an international agency would be limited so that the area inspected 'would not exceed five per cent of the territory under a nation's control or 2,000 square miles, whichever is larger.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys could be done 'on consent of a nation or when specifically authorized' and may be arranged in defined periods (text mentions surveys 'conducted in periods of two years'). Limits intended to constrain intrusiveness of inspections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Council power to investigate and member obligation to cooperate
rubrics_metrics.description: The Security Council 'has the power to make investigations' and 'countries are obligated to co-operate' with such inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. delegates argued that failure to cooperate would 'lay the non-complying states open to serious action to insure their co-operation'; the statement frames investigation and cooperation as enforceable expectations under UN practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Chapter VI and Chapter VII (binding force/enforcement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dispute over legal effect: some delegates argued commissions under Chapter VI can only make recommendations, while Chapter VII provides for enforcement measures including sanctions and use of force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soviet delegate contended the Council could only make recommendations under Chapter VI; U.S. warned that refusal to cooperate could lead to Chapter VII action — the debate bears on whether Council decisions are binding or merely recommendatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereignty exception to cooperation
rubrics_metrics.description: A nation may refuse to co-operate with a commission if it finds that 'the work of a commission is incompatible with its sovereignty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented by the Soviet delegate as a counterpoint to U.S. insistence on obligatory cooperation; raises a legal/political objection states can invoke to block UN measures on sovereignty grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press freedom practices as potential UN membership consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Question raised whether any country that discriminates in news gathering in its territory 'should be a member of the United Nations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument links domestic press practices (denial of visas, censorship, prohibition of imported material) to legitimacy and eligibility for UN membership, implying press freedom as a normative criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural rules for treaty-making (inclusion of nations and veto question)
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. proposal for work on a Japanese peace treaty favored inclusion of 11 nations and denied any single nation's veto; Soviets argued peace treaties should be worked out by the Foreign Ministers Council of the great powers (restoring veto/unanimity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage frames a rubric for treaty-making process: whether to broaden participation and remove veto privileges or restrict to great‑power council and require unanimity — a key procedural standard affecting legitimacy and speed of treaty work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aerial inspection as part of atomic-energy control regime
rubrics_metrics.description: Delegates proposed aerial inspection as 'one phase of a thorough system of inspection to be set up under an international treaty for control of atomic energy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aerial surveys were presented as a technical tool within a broader treaty regime, requiring procedural and scope safeguards (notice, observer rights, area limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recourse to International Court of Justice for interstate disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Security Council recommended that two countries let the International Court of Justice settle their disputes (example: Albania agreeing to appear before the ICJ over British charges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the ICJ to adjudicate interstate disputes was presented as an available and recommended procedural mechanism under UN practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of non-cooperation (political/legal steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: If states refuse to co-operate with Council-established commissions, they 'would be charged in the Security Council' and could face hearings and enforcement measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The newspaper reports warnings that refusal to cooperate could lead to strong enforcement action and further Security Council proceedings — a standard for accountability under UN deliberative practice.
